id_and_class.theory_title: Mitchell and Jennings’s Consciousness Needs a Subject
id_and_class.summary: Kevin J. Mitchell and Carolyn Dicey Jennings argue that to be conscious is to be an experiencing subject: a living being with interests, an integrated self that persists through time. They define this subjecthood by relations (between subject and world, between levels of processing within the subject, and between past and future selves) rather than by any particular computation or biological substrate.
id_and_class.core_identity_tagline: Consciousness as the Mode of Being a Subject

conceptual_ground.explanatory_identity_claim: Consciousness is a mode of being of a subject: an integrated, ‘enminded’ self with interests, continuity, and extension through time.
conceptual_ground.mind_body_relationship: Subjects are living beings, and Jennings argues neuroscience points to an emergent subject that directs attention, defined in natural terms. Mitchell and Jennings hold that what matters is a pattern of relations, not the particular substrate.
conceptual_ground.emergence_type: Emergence of a subject (subjects with interests come first, conceptually and evolutionarily, and consciousness is grounded in them)
conceptual_ground.subjectivity_and_intentionality: Subjectivity is an irreducible first-person stance. When you see red, you are experiencing being yourself seeing red, a self that is a locus of concern as well as a physical point of view.
conceptual_ground.qualia_account: Every quality is experienced by a self: the experience of red is the experience of being you experiencing red, shaped by your memories, attitudes, habits, projects, and interests.
conceptual_ground.ontological_commitments: Living subjects with interests, their ongoing mental organization (memories, dispositions, projects), and relations to the world, among internal levels, and across time.
conceptual_ground.epistemic_access: Conceptual analysis informed by neuroscience, philosophy of attention, and phenomenological work on selfhood (Zahavi, Ganeri).
conceptual_ground.constituents_and_structure: Three kinds of relations make up a conscious mode of being: subject to world, between levels of information processing within the subject, and between temporal parts of the subject (past and future selves).

mechanism_and_dynamics.scope_of_consciousness: Phenomenal subjectivity; selfhood; temporal continuity of the self; agency and interests
mechanism_and_dynamics.distinctive_mechanism_or_principle: Subjecthood as a relational structure: a self that does work to propagate its own dynamic organization into the future.
mechanism_and_dynamics.dynamics_of_emergence: A subject is a process that keeps propagating a pattern into the future. That pattern includes the dynamic organization of the mind as well as the body’s physical arrangement.
mechanism_and_dynamics.location_and_distribution: In the relations of a whole self to its world, among its levels, and across its history, not in a specific brain region.
mechanism_and_dynamics.causation_and_functional_role: The subject is a bundle of interests that acts to sustain itself. Jennings argues the subject directs attention.
mechanism_and_dynamics.integration_or_binding: The self integrates experience across levels of processing and across time, so that consciousness is more than a momentary point of view.
mechanism_and_dynamics.information_flow_or_representation: Relations between levels of information processing within the subject are one of the three relations that ground subjectivity.
mechanism_and_dynamics.evolutionary_account: Subjects with interests came first in evolution, and consciousness developed as a mode of being of such subjects.
core_claims_and_evidence: To be conscious is to be an experiencing subject, a living being with interests.
Subjecthood requires continuity and temporal extension, not just a point of view at a moment.
Conscious beings are ‘enminded’ selves, a deeper condition than embodiment.
Phenomenal subjectivity rests on relations, not on specific computations or substrates.
mechanism_and_dynamics.basis_of_belief_or_evidence_type: Philosophical argument informed by neuroscience and phenomenology

empirics_and_critiques.open_questions_and_limitations: The theory names the relations that make up subjecthood but does not specify how to measure them or what threshold makes a system a subject.
empirics_and_critiques.ontological_coherence: Its substrate neutrality fits functionalist and relational views, while its emphasis on living beings with interests ties it to biology. How those two commitments fit together for artificial systems is left open.

AI_consciousness.rationale: Mitchell and Jennings suggest that artificial entities with the right relations, however implemented, might well be subjects capable of conscious experience.

survival_beyond_death.rationale: Since consciousness is the mode of being of a living subject that works to propagate itself, it ends when that self-sustaining organization stops.

meaning_and_purpose.rationale: Meaning lies in the subject’s own interests, projects, and concerns, with no cosmic purpose implied.

virtual_immortality.rationale: Substrate neutrality leaves room for it in principle, but the view stresses a self’s continuity with its past and future, and Mitchell and Jennings do not say whether a copy would carry that continuity.

sources_and_references.title_with_names: Mitchell and Jennings’s Consciousness Needs a Subject, Landscape of Consciousness, Robert Lawrence Kuhn
